theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of a business proposal?
options: To record the firm's results for the past financial year
To persuade a named reader to approve a course of action
To set out the full history of the firm for new staff
To list every member of staff with their job duties

questions.stem: How does a business proposal usually differ from a business plan?
options: A proposal covers the whole firm for five years
A proposal never includes any costs or prices
A proposal is only ever used inside the firm, never outside it
A proposal seeks a decision on one offer or project

An unsolicited proposal
An internal memo
A five-year business plan

options: Gather data on current use, costs and problems

Choose the most expensive equipment on offer

questions.stem: Where is the executive summary placed in a proposal, and why?
options: At the end, so the reader finishes on the price
In the appendix, where only technical readers will look for it
In the middle, straight after the method section
At the front, so busy readers grasp the case quickly

questions.stem: When is it usually best to write the executive summary?
options: Before any of the research or costing has been done
Before the title page is designed
After the rest of the proposal is drafted
After the client has made its decision

questions.stem: Which objective is written in SMART form?

questions.stem: Why does a proposal state its scope clearly?

One benefit in a proposal is better staff morale. How should this be handled in the cost-benefit section?

questions.stem: Which is the best way to present risks in a proposal?

questions.stem: Which tool best shows the stages and timing of a proposed project on one page?

options: Cut the price by half there and then

questions.stem: What belongs in the appendices of a proposal?

options: That the price can never change at all

questions.stem: What does the 'value proposition' in a proposal explain?

questions.stem: Which question is part of checking whether a proposal is feasible?
options: Do we have the skills, time and money to deliver it?
Is the cover design bright enough to stand out on the client's desk?

questions.stem: A proposal to change a school canteen supplier in Spanish Town will affect students, parents and staff. What should the writer do?
options: Consult the principal and no one else

options: By saying the client will surely be pleased

By naming indicators, targets and review dates

questions.stem: Which visual best compares the costs of three options in a proposal?
options: A bar chart

questions.stem: A community group in Port Antonio is applying for a grant. What must its proposal match most closely?
options: The group's own list of everything it wants

questions.stem: Several people are editing one proposal. What helps most to avoid sending the wrong version?
options: Each writer keeps a private copy of the file

questions.stem: A client accepts a proposal. What normally follows before work starts?
options: The proposal is thrown away as no longer needed

essays.stem: Outline the main sections of a business proposal and explain what each section should do for the reader.
essays.modelAnswer: A proposal opens with a title page and, for longer documents, a contents list. The executive summary comes next: in half a page it states the need, the proposed solution, the cost, the main benefits and what the reader is asked to approve, so a busy decision-maker can grasp the case at once. The background or statement of need shows that the writer understands the client's problem, using facts and figures. The proposed solution sets out what will be done, the scope (what is and is not included), and why this option beats the others considered. The method and timeline explain how and when the work will be done, often with a Gantt chart and milestones. The costs section gives a clear budget with assumptions, GCT where it applies and how long prices are valid. A benefits and risks section shows the return, the risks and how they will be managed. The firm's capability gives evidence it can deliver. The close states the next steps, and appendices hold the detailed support.
markingPoints: Executive summary at the front: need, solution, cost, benefits and the decision asked for
Statement of need showing understanding of the client's problem
Solution and scope, with reasons it beats other options
Method, timeline, costs (with assumptions) and benefits/risks sections
Capability evidence, next steps and appendices

essays.stem: Describe how you would research a client's needs before writing a proposal to provide a staff health programme for a manufacturer in Spanish Town.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin with a meeting with the client's human resources manager and a production manager to learn why they want a programme: for example, high sick leave, injuries or low morale. I would ask for facts such as days lost to sickness in the past year, the number of staff on each shift, their age range and any existing health benefits, and agree how personal information will be protected. I would ask what budget range and timescale they have in mind and who will make the final decision, and what they will judge the proposal on. With permission, I would visit the plant to see the shift pattern, the canteen and break areas, since these affect when sessions can run. A short anonymous staff survey could show what workers would join, such as health checks or fitness sessions. I would also look at what similar firms offer and what local providers charge. From this research I can write a statement of need in the client's own terms and design a programme that fits their shifts and budget.
markingPoints: Meets the client to establish the reasons and goals behind the request
Collects facts and figures (sick leave, staff numbers, shifts), protecting personal data
Finds out budget, timescale, decision-maker and decision criteria
Uses a site visit and/or staff survey to understand practical needs
Uses the research to write the statement of need and fit the solution to the client

essays.stem: A proposal to computerise a firm's stock records costs J$2,400,000 and is expected to save J$800,000 a year for five years. Calculate the simple payback period and the total net saving over five years, and explain how you would present the financial case.
essays.modelAnswer: The simple payback period is the cost divided by the yearly saving: J$2,400,000 divided by J$800,000 equals 3 years. Over five years the total saving is 5 times J$800,000, which is J$4,000,000. Taking away the cost of J$2,400,000 leaves a total net saving of J$1,600,000. I would present this in a simple table showing the cost in year 0, the saving each year, and the running total, so the reader sees the point in year 3 where the system has paid for itself. A short bar or line chart would make this clear at a glance. I would state the assumptions behind the saving, such as fewer stock losses and less staff time on counts, and show what happens if the savings are 20% lower, as a sensitivity check. I would note any costs not included, such as staff training time, and remind the reader of benefits that are hard to price, such as faster, more accurate stock information for managers.
markingPoints: Correct payback: J$2,400,000 ÷ J$800,000 = 3 years
Presents the figures clearly in a table and/or chart with a running total
States assumptions and tests them (sensitivity, e.g. lower savings)
Notes costs left out and non-financial benefits

essays.stem: Evaluate the techniques that make a business proposal persuasive without overstating the case.
essays.modelAnswer: The strongest technique is to start from the reader's need, not the seller's product: when the proposal restates the client's problem in their own terms, the reader feels understood and reads on. Evidence then carries the case. Figures, results from a pilot or past projects, and references from clients persuade far more than adjectives such as 'best' or 'world-class', which a careful reader will distrust. A clear structure with an executive summary and headings helps the reader follow the argument and find what matters to them. Showing the options considered, and why one was chosen, makes the recommendation look fair rather than pushy. Being open about risks and how they will be managed also builds trust, as long as it is balanced. Visuals such as a payback chart make benefits easy to see. Overstating the case is risky: promises that cannot be kept may win a contract but lead to disputes and a damaged name. The best proposals are confident, specific and honest.
markingPoints: Starts from the reader's need and uses the reader's terms
Uses evidence (figures, pilots, past results, references) rather than empty claims
Clear structure and visuals make the argument easy to follow
Shows options and is open about risks, which builds trust
Evaluates the danger of overstating (broken promises, disputes, reputation)

essays.stem: Explain how a proposal should identify and present risks, using a proposal to run a tour service from the cruise port in Falmouth as your example.
essays.modelAnswer: The writer should first list what could stop the tour service meeting its targets. For Falmouth these might include fewer ship calls than expected, bad weather or hurricanes, vehicle breakdowns, accidents on the road, a rival cutting prices, and changes in permits or licensing for tour operators. Each risk is then rated for how likely it is and how serious its impact would be, often as low, medium or high, so the reader can see which matter most. For each important risk the proposal gives a response: for example, agreements with more than one cruise line, a weather policy with refunds or other dates, servicing and spare vehicles, trained drivers and proper insurance, and a clear pricing strategy. The risks are best shown in a simple table, a risk register, with the risk, likelihood, impact, response and the person responsible. Presenting risks honestly in this way shows the client or investor that the team has thought ahead, which makes the proposal more credible rather than weaker.
markingPoints: Identifies realistic risks for the example (ship calls, weather, vehicles, safety, competition, permits)
Rates each risk for likelihood and impact
Gives a practical response for the main risks, including insurance and safety
Presents risks in a clear table or risk register with owners
Explains that honest risk presentation increases credibility

essays.stem: Compare writing a solicited proposal in reply to a public body's tender with writing an unsolicited proposal to a private firm.
essays.modelAnswer: A solicited proposal answers a request, so the client has already accepted that there is a need. The tender documents set the format, page limits, evaluation criteria and closing date, and the procurement rules for public bodies require that every bidder is treated equally. The writer's task is to comply exactly, answer every requirement in the order asked, provide all the forms and certificates required, and show clearly how the bid scores against each criterion. Late or incomplete bids are usually rejected, and there is little room to negotiate. An unsolicited proposal goes to a private firm that has not asked for it, so the writer must first convince the reader that a problem or opportunity exists and is worth their time. There is freedom in format and length, but the proposal must be short, eye-catching and clearly linked to the firm's own goals, and it often follows an earlier conversation. Unsolicited proposals have a lower success rate, but they face no direct competitors and can open new business.
markingPoints: Solicited: need already accepted; format, criteria and deadline set by the tender
Public body: equal treatment under the procurement rules; full compliance; late bids rejected
Unsolicited: must first prove the need or opportunity exists
Unsolicited: freedom of format, but must be brief and linked to the firm's goals
Compares success rates and competition

essays.stem: Describe a review process a team should use before a major proposal is submitted.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should plan review time into the schedule from the start, rather than leaving it to the last night. The first review checks compliance: someone not involved in writing goes through the request for proposals line by line and ticks off where each requirement, form and certificate is answered. The second review checks the content as the client would see it: is the need understood, is the solution clear, are the benefits and evidence convincing, and does the executive summary stand alone? It helps to score the draft against the client's own evaluation criteria. The third review checks the figures: someone with finance skills recalculates every total, checks that GCT and assumptions are shown correctly and that the price matches across all sections. A final proofread looks for spelling, numbering, page limits and formatting, and checks that the right version of every file is attached. A senior manager then signs off the proposal, confirming that the firm can deliver what it promises at the price stated.
markingPoints: Plans review time into the schedule
Compliance review against every requirement by someone not involved in writing
Content review from the client's viewpoint, scored against the evaluation criteria
Finance check: recalculates totals, GCT, assumptions, consistent prices
Final proofread, right version and senior sign-off on deliverability

essays.stem: Your proposal has been shortlisted and you must present it to the client's panel. Plan how you would prepare, and how you would handle questions and objections.
essays.modelAnswer: I would find out how long we have, who sits on the panel and what each member cares about, for example finance, operations or the community. I would build a short presentation around the client's need, our solution, the key figures, the main risks and our ask, with no more than about ten slides, and decide who in our team presents each part. We would rehearse at least twice against the clock. To prepare for questions, the team would list the hardest likely objections, such as price, timing, our size or past experience, and agree short, honest answers with evidence. On the day, I would listen to each question fully, thank the person, and answer briefly and directly. If the objection is price, I would explain the value and payback, and offer options such as phasing rather than cutting the price on the spot. If I do not know an answer, I would say so and promise a written reply by a set time. Afterwards we would send a short thank-you letter with any follow-up information.
markingPoints: Researches the panel, time allowed and members' interests
Prepares a short, focused presentation and rehearses with set roles
Lists likely objections and prepares evidence-based answers
Handles questions calmly: listen, thank, answer briefly; use value, payback or options for price
Admits unknowns, promises follow-up, and sends a thank-you with information afterwards

essays.stem: Explain the ethical and legal points a proposal writer must keep in mind, including honesty, confidentiality, ownership of ideas and gifts.
essays.modelAnswer: Honesty comes first. A proposal is the basis of a later contract, so every claim about experience, staff, results and prices must be true and checkable, and any assumptions must be stated. Promising more than the firm can deliver may lead to disputes, penalties under the contract and a damaged reputation. Confidentiality works both ways: the writer must protect information the client shares, such as figures or plans, and must not use it for any other purpose. The firm should also mark its own sensitive material as confidential. Ownership of ideas matters, because the firm's designs, methods and written material are protected in general by intellectual property law; the proposal can state that they remain the firm's property unless agreed otherwise, and the writer must not copy other people's work or photographs without permission. Gifts or favours offered to officers who influence the decision can amount to bribery and, for public bodies, break the procurement rules, so the writer must refuse and report any such request. Any conflict of interest must be declared.
markingPoints: Honesty: true, checkable claims and stated assumptions; dangers of overpromising
Confidentiality of the client's information and the firm's own sensitive material
Ownership of ideas: protect the firm's work and do not copy others' (intellectual property law in general)
Gifts and favours: refuse and report; links to bribery and procurement rules
Declares conflicts of interest

essays.stem: Justify why a firm should review every proposal after the decision, whether it wins or loses, and describe how it should do so.
essays.modelAnswer: Proposals cost a great deal of staff time, so a firm should learn from each one in order to raise its success rate and avoid bidding for work it is unlikely to win. A win can hide weaknesses, such as a price set too low or promises that will be hard to keep, while a loss often contains lessons about price, evidence or presentation. The review should start by asking the client for feedback; many clients, and public bodies in particular, will give a debrief on how the bid scored against each criterion. Within two weeks, the bid team should meet for a short, blame-free review covering what went well, what did not, how accurate the costing was and whether the timeline for writing worked. Lessons should be written down and added to a shared library together with good sections, CVs, case studies and standard answers that can be reused. The firm should also track its win rate and the cost of bidding over the year, and use this to decide which future opportunities to pursue.
markingPoints: Justifies review: cost of bidding, raising win rate, lessons from wins and losses
Asks the client for a debrief or feedback against the criteria
Holds a short, blame-free team review soon after the decision
Records lessons and builds a reusable library of content
Tracks win rate and bid costs to guide future decisions

practical1.title: Write a business proposal in reply to a request for proposals
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a short request for proposals (RFP), for example from a municipal corporation that wants a recycling service at its market, or from a hotel that wants a staff customer-service training programme. As a group, write a proposal of 4 to 6 pages that answers the RFP in full. Give each member a named role and a named section: bid manager and editor (plan, timetable and executive summary), researcher (statement of need and solution), costing officer (budget with assumptions, contingency and GCT shown 'at the current rate'), timeline and risk officer (Gantt chart and risk table), and compliance reviewer (checklist matching every RFP requirement to a page). In a group of four, the bid manager also does the compliance check. Use only figures given or worked out by the group, and check every sum twice. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with word processor and spreadsheet software, and a printer
Proposal and compliance checklist templates (or blank paper)
photos: The group's planning sheet showing roles, sections and a writing timetable
The draft budget table with assumptions and contingency, on screen or printed
The Gantt chart and the risk table
The completed compliance checklist matched to page numbers
The finished proposal: cover, executive summary page and contents page
checklist: Took a named role and wrote or checked their named section
Section answers the RFP's requirements in the order asked and keeps to the page limit
Figures are correct and clearly set out, with assumptions and GCT shown at the current rate (no rate invented)
Writing is clear, professional and persuasive, with no unsupported claims
Gantt chart shows tasks, dates and milestones; risk table shows likelihood, impact and response
Took part in the compliance and proofreading review and corrected faults found
Met the group's internal deadline and helped hand in one final version
safety: Use only the RFP and made-up details; do not copy text or images from other firms' documents
Keep the group's draft confidential to the group and the assessor
Share the workload fairly and agree deadlines that are realistic
Take short breaks from the screen and keep cables tidy around the computers

practical2.title: Present and defend an internal proposal to a management panel
practical2.brief: Your group works for a medium-sized firm (the assessor gives the details). Prepare an internal proposal asking senior management to approve and fund one improvement, for example moving paper records to a digital system or setting up a staff wellness programme. Produce a two-page written proposal and a set of no more than 8 slides. Give each member a named role: lead presenter, finance lead (costs, payback and benefit-cost ratio), operations lead (how it will work and the timeline), risk and objections lead (prepares answers to likely objections), and note-taker (records the panel's questions and the agreed changes). Present for 10 minutes to a panel (the assessor and members of another group), then answer questions for 10 minutes. Every member must speak. Afterwards, revise the written proposal to deal with the panel's main objection and hand in both versions. Photograph each stage.
materials: Computers with word processor, spreadsheet and presentation software
photos: The slides, printed as handouts or shown on screen
The group presenting to the panel
The note-taker's record of questions and objections
The revised proposal with the change marked
checklist: Took a named role and spoke during the presentation or the questions
Figures for cost, payback and benefit-cost ratio are correct and explained simply
Linked the proposal to the firm's goals and the panel's concerns
Answered questions honestly and calmly, with evidence, without cutting the price on the spot
Kept to the time limit and used slides that are clear and uncluttered
Helped revise the proposal in response to the panel's main objection
safety: Treat panel members and other groups with respect; criticise ideas, not people
Use made-up company figures only; no real confidential data
Check projector and extension leads are placed so no one trips
Keep workload fair and take short breaks between preparing and presenting
